title: Quality-related Events and the Reports They Trigger
topic: Quality assurance and mandatory reporting / Sorting a quality-related event into the right track
subtopic: The CQI Program and its six minimum provisions in 247 CMR 15.02(1), the discovery, notification, 24-hour documentation and analysis sequence in 247 CMR 15.03, the CQI records and two-year QRE retention in 247 CMR 15.04, the seven-business-day serious-event reports and five-year records in 247 CMR 20.02 with the non-resident carve-out from its reporting requirements and the replacement duty in 247 CMR 20.07(3), and the Massachusetts theft or loss reports to the Board, to the Drug Control Program and to the police
learning_objectives: List the six minimum provisions a CQI Program shall include under 247 CMR 15.02(1) and identify which of them a bare incident log leaves undone.
Separate the escalation duty that 247 CMR 15.03(1) places on all pharmacy personnel from the three-part immediate response it places on the pharmacist.
State the 24-hour QRE documentation deadline, name what starts it, and reproduce the four content elements required by 247 CMR 15.03(2)(b).
Distinguish the analysis half of 247 CMR 15.03(3) from its response half, and say what each one requires.
Apply the seven-business-day period in 247 CMR 20.02(1) and explain why it runs from discovery of the serious injury or death rather than from the dispensing.
Contrast 247 CMR 20.02(1) with 247 CMR 20.02(2) on the event, the recipients and the trigger that starts the clock.
Explain why a complete QRE record never discharges a Board report, using the words of 247 CMR 20.02(3).
Measure the five-year serious-event retention from the correct date and state the readily retrievable standard that accompanies it.
State the two-year QRE retention in 247 CMR 15.04(2), the date it runs from, and the other records 247 CMR 15.04 requires, and keep it apart from the five-year serious-event period.

Apply the non-resident carve-out in 247 CMR 20.02(5) to the reporting requirements it names, say what 247 CMR 20.07(1) leaves in place, and use the different duty and trigger that 247 CMR 20.07(3) supplies.

Route a theft, loss or suspected tampering of controlled substances to every recipient Massachusetts names, including the police copies M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15 ties to a DEA Form 106, on the correct instrument and within the correct period.
Sort a single set of facts into the CQI track, the Board reporting track, the Drug Control Program track, or more than one of them at once.

orientation.text: 247 CMR 15.02(1) requires each pharmacy to establish a Continuous Quality Improvement Program, and it states the purpose of that programme in four verbs: detecting, documenting, assessing and preventing Quality Related Events. The regulation then fixes a floor beneath the programme. At a minimum a CQI Program shall include provisions to designate an individual or individuals responsible for monitoring CQI Program compliance with the requirements of 247 CMR 15.00, to identify and document QREs, to minimise the impact of QREs on patients, to analyse data collected in response to QREs to assess causes and any contributing factors, to use the findings of that analysis to formulate an appropriate response and develop pharmacy systems and workflow processes designed to prevent QREs, and to provide ongoing education at least annually in the area of CQI to pharmacy personnel. Six provisions, not one. A pharmacy that keeps an incident log and does nothing else has satisfied the second of them and left the other five undone.

The programme is a standing structure. 247 CMR 15.03 is what happens when an event actually occurs, and its first subsection carries two duties that are easy to read as one. All pharmacy personnel shall be trained to bring any QRE to the attention of the pharmacist on duty or the pharmacist Manager of Record immediately upon discovery, so the escalation duty reaches the whole staff rather than pharmacists alone. The pharmacist who has discovered or been informed of a QRE shall then immediately provide notification to the patient or the patient's representative, the prescriber if indicated in the professional judgment of the pharmacist, and other members of the healthcare team; directions for correcting the error; and instructions for minimising the negative impact on the patient. Three things are owed rather than one, and the regulation prescribes no sequence among them. The professional-judgment qualifier is the single discretionary element in the subsection, and it attaches to the prescriber notification alone. Notification of the patient or the patient's representative is not conditioned on it.

247 CMR 15.03(2) puts a clock on the paperwork and then says what the paperwork must contain. A QRE shall be initially documented by the pharmacist who has discovered or been informed of it within 24 hours after the QRE is discovered by or described to the pharmacist. Two features of that deadline decide questions. The period is 24 hours and not one business day, so it runs across nights, weekends and holidays. And it starts at discovery or description, so it does not wait for the patient to confirm harm and it is not measured from the dispensing that went wrong. The documentation itself must describe the event sufficiently to permit categorisation and analysis of it, and must include the date when the pharmacist discovered or received notification of the QRE together with the name of the person who notified the pharmacy, the names and titles of the persons recording the QRE information and performing the QRE analysis, a description of the QRE reviewed, and documentation of the contact with the patient or the patient's representative, the prescribing practitioner if indicated in the professional judgment of the pharmacist, and other members of the healthcare team.

247 CMR 15.03(3) closes the loop, and its two halves are separately examinable. Under the analysis half, the investigative and other pertinent data collected in response to QREs shall be analysed, individually and collectively, to assess the cause and any contributing factors such as system or process failures. The analysis and assessment shall include a consideration of the effects on quality assurance related to workflow processes, technological support, personnel training and staffing levels; any recommended remedial changes to pharmacy policies, procedures, systems or processes; and the development of indicators that identify means against which a pharmacy's program intends to measure its standards over a designated period of time. Under the response half, each pharmacy shall inform pharmacy personnel of changes to pharmacy policies, procedures, systems or processes resulting from recommendations generated by the CQI Program. An analysis whose conclusions never reach the staff who do the work leaves the second half undone, however thorough the first half was.

247 CMR 15.04 closes the CQI regulation with the records it leaves behind, and it answers the retention question a candidate is most likely to ask. Each pharmacy shall maintain a written copy of its CQI Program description on the pharmacy premises, and that description shall be readily available to all pharmacy personnel, so the programme is a document on site rather than a set of habits. Each pharmacy shall maintain a record of all QREs for a minimum period of two years from the date of the QRE report. Read the start point carefully, because it is the date of the QRE report and not the date of the event, the date of the dispensing or the date any Board report was filed. QRE records shall be maintained in an orderly manner and filed by date, which is a condition on how they are kept rather than on how long. And QRE records may be stored at a site other than the pharmacy where the QRE occurred, so an off-site archive is permitted even though the written CQI Program description must be on the premises.

Everything to this point stays inside the pharmacy. 247 CMR 20.02 is where an event leaves the building, and it describes two reports rather than one. Under 247 CMR 20.02(1) a Manager of Record of a pharmacy shall report to the Board any improper dispensing of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death, within seven business days of discovery of serious injury or death related to improper dispensing. Under 247 CMR 20.02(2) a Manager of Record shall report any serious adverse drug event that occurs as a result of a patient's interaction with any drug or pharmaceutical manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy, and that report goes to three recipients: the Board, the Federal Food and Drug Administration MedWatch Program, and the Betsy Lehman Center for Patient Safety and Medical Error Reduction. Its period is also seven business days, but it runs from the knowledge of the serious adverse drug event by any pharmacy employee rather than from the Manager of Record's own discovery. 247 CMR 20.02(3) then closes the obvious shortcut: the duty to report to the Board improper dispensing of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death, or a serious adverse drug event, shall be in addition to the Continuous Quality Improvement Program requirements of 247 CMR 15.00.

Before applying any of 247 CMR 20.02, ask which pharmacy the facts are about, because 247 CMR 20.02(5) provides that the reporting requirements in 247 CMR 20.02 do not apply to non-resident pharmacies. Read those words closely, because they name a subset of what 247 CMR 20.02 contains rather than the whole of it: the reporting duties in 20.02(1) and 20.02(2), and the statement in 20.02(3) about how those duties sit alongside 247 CMR 15.00, are what the sentence reaches. The carve-out is not a gap in the scheme either. 247 CMR 20.07(1) requires a non-resident pharmacy, non-resident sterile compounding pharmacy and non-resident complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy to comply with all provisions of 247 CMR 20.00 unless otherwise provided, and 247 CMR 20.07(3) states the duty that replaces 20.02(1) for them. A non-resident pharmacy shall report to the Board any improper dispensing, into Massachusetts, of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death within seven business days of discovery of the improper dispensing. The length is the same and the recipient is the same, but the trigger is not. The resident pharmacy's clock runs from discovery of the serious injury or death, and the non-resident pharmacy's runs from discovery of the improper dispensing, so the same facts can produce two different start dates depending on where the pharmacy sits.

How far that carve-out reaches decides a records question, so settle it before the retention rules arrive. 247 CMR 20.02(4) is a retention requirement rather than a reporting requirement: it says how long a pharmacy keeps records and how retrievable it keeps them, and it directs no report to anyone. Since 247 CMR 20.02(5) sets aside the reporting requirements in 247 CMR 20.02, and 247 CMR 20.07(1) leaves every provision of 247 CMR 20.00 on a non-resident pharmacy unless otherwise provided, the better reading is that 20.02(4) survives for a non-resident pharmacy, with its five years running from the date that pharmacy's 247 CMR 20.07(3) report is filed with the Board. Be honest that the sentence can be pressed the other way, because a reader could take the reporting requirements in 247 CMR 20.02 as a loose way of naming the whole of a section whose heading is a duty to report. Two things answer that. The Board wrote a narrowing word where it could have written none, and it is the narrowing word that has to be given work to do. And the two readings do not carry the same risk: a pharmacy that keeps the file for five years has complied whichever reading is right, while a pharmacy that destroys it earlier has no answer at all if the narrower reading is the correct one.

A reportable event leaves a longer paper trail than the report itself. 247 CMR 20.02(4) requires a pharmacy to retain all records relating to the improper dispensing of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death, and all records relating to serious adverse drug events, for a minimum period of five years from the date the report is filed with the Board, and it adds that the records shall be readily retrievable. Two details in that sentence do the work. The period runs from the filing of the report and not from the dispensing, the injury or the discovery, so delay in filing lengthens the retention rather than shortening it. And readily retrievable is a standard about the manner of keeping and not merely about duration: material that exists somewhere in an unindexed archive has been retained but is not readily retrievable. The five-year period attaches to all records relating to the event, not only to the copy of the report that was filed. And because 247 CMR 20.02(4) states a retention requirement rather than one of the reporting requirements that 247 CMR 20.02(5) sets aside, a non-resident pharmacy keeps the same five-year readily retrievable file, measured from the filing of its own report to the Board.

The third track has nothing to do with the CQI Program. Under 105 CMR 700.008, a Department of Public Health regulation, a registrant shall report the theft, loss or suspected tampering of any controlled substances to the Drug Control Program within the Department within 24 hours of discovery of such theft, loss or suspected tampering, by completing and submitting the form provided or approved by the Drug Control Program for such purpose. Three features separate it from everything else in this section. Suspicion of tampering is itself a trigger, so nothing has to be confirmed missing before the duty attaches. The 24 hours run from discovery rather than from the theft, the loss, or the delivery that later turns out to have been interfered with. And the recipient is the Drug Control Program on its own form, so a report made to the Board of Registration in Pharmacy instead does not answer this regulation. Registrant carries its defined sense here: 105 CMR 700.001 makes it a person registered by the Department under M.G.L. c. 94C, and 105 CMR 700.004(A)(1) read with M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(a) leaves a retail drug business registered with the Board instead, so the 24-hour route reaches an operator such as a hospital directly. Do not turn that into a rule that nobody at a community pharmacy is a registrant, because 105 CMR 700.004(A)(2) lists a Pharmacist among the practitioners required to be registered under 105 CMR 700.004(A)(1), and requires registration separately for each business or professional activity. The pharmacy registers with the Board and the pharmacist registers with the Department, so a duty 105 CMR 700.000 addresses to a registrant can reach the individual pharmacist even where it does not reach the retail drug business in that capacity.

That the Drug Control Program report does not go to the Board is not the same proposition as a theft or loss never going to the Board, and the difference decides questions. 247 CMR 20.03(7) requires a Drug Store pharmacy, sterile compounding pharmacy, complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy or nuclear pharmacy located in Massachusetts to report a theft or loss of a significant amount of controlled substances by submitting to the Board a copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and DEA Form 106 within seven days of such theft or significant loss, and to comply where applicable with the reporting requirements of the DEA, the Department and the state and local police. So a discovered loss of controlled substances at a Massachusetts pharmacy can owe a Board report on a seven-day clock, a Department report on a 24-hour clock where the operator is a Department registrant, and the federal route, which is taught in the section on controlled substance security and disposal. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15 adds the police to that list. Where a person registered to dispense controlled substances discovers a theft or loss that requires the filing of a DEA Form 106 with the United States Drug Enforcement Administration, that person shall simultaneously file a copy of the form with the police department in the city or town wherein the theft or loss is alleged to have occurred and with the department of state police, while a person registered to distribute owes the copy to the department of state police. Those copies travel with the Form 106 rather than on a period of their own. What the 105 CMR 700.008 route rules out is only the substitution of a Board report for the Drug Control Program's form.

Two retention periods run through this material and they are not the same period, so keep them apart by their start points. 247 CMR 15.04(2) gives the ordinary QRE record a minimum of two years from the date of the QRE report, and it reaches every QRE whether or not the event ever becomes reportable to anyone. 247 CMR 20.02(4) gives records relating to a reportable improper dispensing or a serious adverse drug event a minimum of five years from the date the report is filed with the Board, together with a readily retrievable standard the CQI provision does not state. A single serious event therefore sits inside both: the QRE record it generated runs two years from the QRE report, and the wider file of records relating to the event runs five years from the filing. One boundary is worth fixing as well, because it is a place where a plausible proposition would have to come from outside these rules. Nothing in 247 CMR 15.00 makes a QRE record confidential, privileged or shielded from discovery, so this section teaches no such protection, and the internal character of the record is not itself a legal shield. The federal theft-or-loss reporting route is separate law with its own recipient, form and trigger, and it belongs to its own section rather than to this one.

worked_examples.scenario: A technician notices at 9 a.m. on a Tuesday that a prescription dispensed the previous Friday carried the wrong strength, and she tells the pharmacist on duty at once. By midday the pharmacy learns that the patient suffered a serious injury related to the error and was admitted to hospital overnight. The Manager of Record concludes that a complete CQI file answers the whole matter, because the incident is thoroughly documented inside the pharmacy.
steps: Take the escalation first. 247 CMR 15.03(1) requires all pharmacy personnel to be trained to bring any QRE to the attention of the pharmacist on duty or the pharmacist Manager of Record immediately upon discovery, and that is what the technician did.

Run the pharmacist's immediate duties under 247 CMR 15.03(1): notification to the patient or the patient's representative, to the prescriber if indicated in the professional judgment of the pharmacist and to other members of the healthcare team, directions for correcting the error, and instructions for minimising the negative impact on the patient.

Start the documentation clock at 9 a.m. Tuesday. 247 CMR 15.03(2)(a) requires initial documentation within 24 hours after the QRE is discovered by or described to the pharmacist, and the content elements in 247 CMR 15.03(2)(b) belong to that record rather than to a later write-up.

Start the second clock separately. Under 247 CMR 20.02(1) the Manager of Record reports the improper dispensing to the Board within seven business days of discovery of the serious injury related to it, so that period begins at midday on Tuesday and not at Friday's dispensing.

Reject the shortcut on the regulation's own words. 247 CMR 20.02(3) provides that the duty to report to the Board is in addition to the Continuous Quality Improvement Program requirements of 247 CMR 15.00.

Fix the retention. 247 CMR 20.02(4) requires all records relating to the improper dispensing to be retained a minimum of five years from the date the report is filed with the Board, and to be readily retrievable.
worked_examples.resolution: Both tracks run: an immediate response and 24-hour QRE documentation inside the pharmacy, and a separate seven-business-day Board report by the Manager of Record whose records are then kept five years from filing. The error the scenario invites is treating a complete internal CQI file as a substitute for the Board report, with a second error close behind it, which is dating the seven business days from Friday's dispensing rather than from discovery of the serious injury.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy compounds an oral suspension on its own premises. On a Monday a pharmacy technician takes a telephone call from a parent describing a severe reaction in a child who received it, and she writes the call up in the pharmacy's log. The Manager of Record is on leave and first reads the log entry on the following Thursday. He intends to notify the Board within seven business days of Thursday and to treat that notification as the whole of the reporting obligation.
steps: Classify the event on the regulation's own terms. 247 CMR 20.02(2) reaches a serious adverse drug event occurring as a result of a patient's interaction with any drug or pharmaceutical manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy, and the suspension was compounded there.

Date the clock correctly. 247 CMR 20.02(2) runs seven business days from the knowledge of the serious adverse drug event by any pharmacy employee, so the period started on the Monday the technician took the call and not on the Thursday the Manager of Record read the log.

Count the recipients. 247 CMR 20.02(2) directs the report to the Board, to the Federal Food and Drug Administration MedWatch Program and to the Betsy Lehman Center for Patient Safety and Medical Error Reduction, so a notification to the Board alone leaves two recipients unserved.

Keep the internal track running alongside it, because 247 CMR 20.02(3) makes the reporting duty additional to the Continuous Quality Improvement Program requirements of 247 CMR 15.00 rather than a replacement for them.

Apply the retention standard. 247 CMR 20.02(4) requires all records relating to serious adverse drug events to be kept a minimum period of five years from the date the report is filed with the Board, and to be readily retrievable.
worked_examples.resolution: The period had been running since Monday and was not restarted when the Manager of Record read the log on Thursday, and the report is owed to three recipients rather than one. The error the scenario invites is running an employee-knowledge clock from the responsible individual's own knowledge, and behind it the assumption that a serious-event report under 247 CMR 20.02 has a single recipient.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts registrant takes delivery of a controlled substances shipment on a Wednesday. The following Monday morning a pharmacist opening the safe notices that one carton inside that shipment appears to have been opened and resealed. The perpetual inventory shows no shortfall. The Manager of Record proposes to spend the week reconciling counts and then to notify the Board of Registration in Pharmacy if a loss is confirmed.
steps: Identify the trigger in 105 CMR 700.008. It reaches the theft, loss or suspected tampering of any controlled substances, so suspected tampering stands on its own footing and does not wait for a confirmed shortfall.
Date the clock from discovery. The regulation gives 24 hours of discovery of such theft, loss or suspected tampering, so the period runs from Monday morning rather than from the Wednesday delivery.

Send the report to the right recipient. 105 CMR 700.008 directs it to the Drug Control Program within the Department, so a notification to the Board of Registration in Pharmacy does not answer this regulation.

Use the right instrument. The report is made by completing and submitting the form provided or approved by the Drug Control Program for such purpose, so an internal memorandum or a note in the CQI file is not the report.

Ask separately whether the Board is owed anything, rather than concluding from 105 CMR 700.008 that it is not. If the facts turn out to involve a theft or loss of a significant amount of controlled substances at a Massachusetts Drug Store, sterile compounding, complex non-sterile compounding or nuclear pharmacy, 247 CMR 20.03(7) requires a copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and DEA Form 106 to reach the Board within seven days of that theft or significant loss.

Keep the boundary in view. Whether these facts also constitute a quality-related event turns on a definition the rules underlying this section do not carry, and the federal theft-or-loss reporting route is separate law taught in its own section.
worked_examples.resolution: A report goes to the Drug Control Program on its own form within 24 hours of Monday's discovery, whatever the reconciliation later shows, and if the reconciliation establishes a significant loss the Board is owed its own report within seven days. The error the scenario invites is treating confirmation of a loss as the trigger, compounded by running the clock from the delivery and by sending the Drug Control Program's report to the Board instead; the mirror-image error is reading that misdirection as proof that the Board hears nothing at all.

worked_examples.scenario: A community pharmacy opened 18 months ago. It keeps a bound incident log, it has named its Manager of Record as the individual responsible for monitoring CQI Program compliance, and it reviews the log at a monthly meeting at which the pharmacist owner decides what to change. Staff learn of the changes when a new prompt appears on the dispensing screen. Every pharmacist on staff has completed continuing education in pharmacy law this year, and the owner treats that as the pharmacy's CQI education.
steps: Test the programme against the floor in 247 CMR 15.02(1). The designation required by 15.02(1)(a) and the identification and documentation of QREs required by 15.02(1)(b) are in place, so the question is which of the remaining minimum provisions are not.

Apply 247 CMR 15.03(3)(a). The analysis and assessment must include a consideration of the effects on quality assurance related to workflow processes, technological support, personnel training and staffing levels, any recommended remedial changes to policies, procedures, systems or processes, and the development of indicators that identify means against which the programme intends to measure its standards over a designated period of time.

Apply 247 CMR 15.03(3)(b). Each pharmacy shall inform pharmacy personnel of changes to pharmacy policies, procedures, systems or processes resulting from recommendations generated by the CQI Program, so leaving staff to discover a new screen prompt does not discharge the response half.

Apply 247 CMR 15.02(1)(f). The programme must provide ongoing education at least annually in the area of CQI to pharmacy personnel, and the audience named is pharmacy personnel rather than pharmacists alone.

Separate the two education duties. An individual pharmacist's continuing education is governed elsewhere and is not what 247 CMR 15.02(1)(f) requires; the annual CQI education is a provision of the pharmacy's own programme and stands or falls on its own.
worked_examples.resolution: The programme is incomplete on at least three counts: the analysis lacks the indicators that 247 CMR 15.03(3)(a) requires, the response is never communicated to pharmacy personnel as 247 CMR 15.03(3)(b) requires, and no annual CQI education has been provided. The error the scenario invites is treating an incident log plus a named compliance monitor as a complete CQI Program, and treating pharmacists' individual continuing education as the pharmacy's annual CQI education.

worked_examples.scenario: A mail-order pharmacy licensed in another state and holding a Massachusetts non-resident licence dispenses a prescription into Massachusetts on 3 March. Its staff discover the dispensing error on 10 March and learn on 24 March that the patient was seriously injured. The Manager of Record intends to count seven business days from 24 March, and to purge the pharmacy's file two years after the Board report goes in.
steps: Check what 247 CMR 20.02 still does here. 247 CMR 20.02(5) provides that the reporting requirements in 247 CMR 20.02 do not apply to non-resident pharmacies, so the reporting rule the Manager of Record is counting from is not the one that governs this pharmacy. Note what the sentence names, though: the reporting requirements in 247 CMR 20.02 rather than the whole of it.

Find the provision that does apply. 247 CMR 20.07(1) makes a non-resident pharmacy comply with all provisions of 247 CMR 20.00 unless otherwise provided, and 247 CMR 20.07(3) requires it to report to the Board any improper dispensing, into Massachusetts, of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death within seven business days of discovery of the improper dispensing.

Date the clock from the right event. The trigger under 20.07(3) is discovery of the improper dispensing, which was 10 March, not discovery of the serious injury on 24 March, so the period has been running for two weeks longer than the Manager of Record supposes.

Separate the two retention periods rather than merging them, and give each one its own source. 247 CMR 15.04(2) requires the record of the QRE to be kept a minimum of two years from the date of the QRE report. 247 CMR 20.02(4) requires all records relating to the improper dispensing to be kept a minimum of five years from the date the report is filed with the Board, and to be readily retrievable; it is a retention requirement and not one of the reporting requirements named in 20.02(5), and 247 CMR 20.07(1) makes this pharmacy comply with all provisions of 247 CMR 20.00 unless otherwise provided, so it binds here too.

Work out what may actually be purged, and when. The two-year figure in 247 CMR 15.04(2) is a minimum period rather than a destruction date, and it covers the QRE record alone. The wider file of records relating to this improper dispensing is held by the five-year period, measured from the day the 247 CMR 20.07(3) report reaches the Board, so nothing in that file may be cleared out at the two-year mark and the readily retrievable standard applies to it throughout.

Keep the internal track running whichever reporting provision applies. 247 CMR 15.00 is not limited by 247 CMR 20.02(5), so the escalation, the immediate response, the 24-hour documentation and the analysis all proceed on their own terms.
worked_examples.resolution: The seven business days ran from 10 March, the discovery of the improper dispensing, so the report fell due well before the Manager of Record supposes. The purge is wrong as well. The QRE record carries a two-year minimum under 247 CMR 15.04(2), but the records relating to this improper dispensing are kept a minimum of five years from the date the report is filed with the Board and must remain readily retrievable, so the file may not be cleared out two years after the report goes in. The errors the scenario invites are carrying the resident pharmacy's trigger onto non-resident facts, and reading 247 CMR 20.02(5) as lifting the whole of 247 CMR 20.02 off the pharmacy when it names only the reporting requirements there.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A QRE must be initially documented within ______, measured from ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: 24 hours; the moment the QRE is discovered by or described to the pharmacist who documents it, under 247 CMR 15.03(2)(a).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the three things the pharmacist who has discovered or been informed of a QRE must immediately provide.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Notification to the patient or the patient's representative, the prescriber if indicated in the professional judgment of the pharmacist, and other members of the healthcare team; directions for correcting the error; and instructions for minimising the negative impact on the patient, under 247 CMR 15.03(1).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 247 CMR 20.02(1) the Manager of Record reports to ______ within ______, measured from ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: the Board; seven business days; discovery of the serious injury or death related to the improper dispensing.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A serious adverse drug event under 247 CMR 20.02(2) is reported to how many recipients, and which ones?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Three: the Board, the Federal Food and Drug Administration MedWatch Program, and the Betsy Lehman Center for Patient Safety and Medical Error Reduction.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: The seven-business-day period in 247 CMR 20.02(2) runs from ______, and not from the Manager of Record's own discovery.
retrieval_prompts.answer: the knowledge of the serious adverse drug event by any pharmacy employee.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Serious-event records are retained for ______, measured from ______, and must be ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: a minimum period of five years; the date the report is filed with the Board; readily retrievable, under 247 CMR 20.02(4).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How long is the record of a QRE kept, and from what date?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A minimum period of two years from the date of the QRE report, under 247 CMR 15.04(2). That is a different start point from the five-year serious-event period, which runs from the date the report is filed with the Board.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the three other things 247 CMR 15.04 requires of a pharmacy besides the two-year QRE retention.
retrieval_prompts.answer: A written copy of the CQI Program description maintained on the pharmacy premises and readily available to all pharmacy personnel; QRE records maintained in an orderly manner and filed by date; and permission to store QRE records at a site other than the pharmacy where the QRE occurred.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does 247 CMR 20.02(5) switch off for a non-resident pharmacy, and what takes its place?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The reporting requirements in 247 CMR 20.02, and nothing wider than that. 247 CMR 20.07(1) requires a non-resident pharmacy to comply with all provisions of 247 CMR 20.00 unless otherwise provided, and 247 CMR 20.07(3) requires it to report to the Board any improper dispensing, into Massachusetts, of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death within seven business days of discovery of the improper dispensing.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Two seven-business-day periods run to the Board on improper dispensing facts. What separates them?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The trigger. For a resident pharmacy under 247 CMR 20.02(1) the period runs from discovery of the serious injury or death; for a non-resident pharmacy under 247 CMR 20.07(3) it runs from discovery of the improper dispensing.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A Massachusetts Drug Store pharmacy discovers a theft of a significant amount of controlled substances. Does anything go to the Board?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Yes. 247 CMR 20.03(7) requires a copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and DEA Form 106 to be submitted to the Board within seven days of the theft or significant loss, and compliance where applicable with the DEA, Department and state and local police requirements. What 105 CMR 700.008 rules out is substituting a Board report for the Drug Control Program's own form.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a report of suspected tampering may wait until a reconciliation confirms that controlled substances are actually missing.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. 105 CMR 700.008 makes suspected tampering a trigger in its own right and allows 24 hours of discovery.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: The theft, loss or suspected tampering report goes to ______, within ______, by ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: the Drug Control Program within the Department; 24 hours of discovery; completing and submitting the form provided or approved by the Drug Control Program for such purpose.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How often must a CQI Program provide education in the area of CQI, and to whom?
retrieval_prompts.answer: At least annually, to pharmacy personnel, under 247 CMR 15.02(1)(f).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: List the four elements that 247 CMR 15.03(2)(b) requires QRE documentation to include.
retrieval_prompts.answer: The date the pharmacist discovered or received notification of the QRE together with the name of the person who notified the pharmacy; the names and titles of the persons recording the QRE information and performing the QRE analysis; a description of the QRE reviewed; and documentation of the contact with the patient or the patient's representative, the prescribing practitioner if indicated in the professional judgment of the pharmacist, and other members of the healthcare team.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Beyond assessing the cause and any contributing factors, what three things must the QRE analysis and assessment include?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A consideration of the effects on quality assurance related to workflow processes, technological support, personnel training and staffing levels; any recommended remedial changes to pharmacy policies, procedures, systems or processes; and the development of indicators that identify means against which the programme intends to measure its standards over a designated period of time, under 247 CMR 15.03(3)(a).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: completing the QRE documentation discharges the Manager of Record's obligation where an improper dispensing has caused serious injury.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. 247 CMR 20.02(3) makes the duty to report to the Board additional to the Continuous Quality Improvement Program requirements of 247 CMR 15.00, so both duties run.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What must a CQI Program designate under 247 CMR 15.02(1)(a)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: An individual or individuals responsible for monitoring CQI Program compliance with the requirements of 247 CMR 15.00.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who must be trained to bring a QRE to the pharmacist on duty or the pharmacist Manager of Record, and how quickly?
retrieval_prompts.answer: All pharmacy personnel, immediately upon discovery, under 247 CMR 15.03(1).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Once the CQI Program generates recommendations that change a pharmacy's procedures, what does 247 CMR 15.03(3)(b) require?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Each pharmacy shall inform pharmacy personnel of the changes to pharmacy policies, procedures, systems or processes resulting from those recommendations.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A non-resident pharmacy has filed its 247 CMR 20.07(3) report. How long does it keep the records relating to that improper dispensing, and on what reasoning?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A minimum period of five years from the date the report is filed with the Board, readily retrievable. 247 CMR 20.02(4) requires records rather than a report, so it is not among the reporting requirements named in 247 CMR 20.02(5), and 247 CMR 20.07(1) keeps every provision of 247 CMR 20.00 on the pharmacy unless otherwise provided.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Besides the Board and the Drug Control Program, who else does Massachusetts name on a theft or loss of controlled substances?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The police. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15 a person registered to dispense controlled substances who must file a DEA Form 106 with the United States Drug Enforcement Administration shall simultaneously file a copy with the police department in the city or town wherein the theft or loss is alleged to have occurred and with the department of state police; a person registered to distribute files the copy with the department of state police.

quick_review.text: 247 CMR 15.02(1) requires each pharmacy to establish a CQI Program for detecting, documenting, assessing and preventing Quality Related Events, and lists six minimum provisions it shall include.
The first of those six provisions designates an individual or individuals responsible for monitoring CQI Program compliance with the requirements of 247 CMR 15.00.
A CQI Program must provide ongoing education at least annually in the area of CQI, and the audience stated in 247 CMR 15.02(1)(f) is pharmacy personnel rather than pharmacists alone.
All pharmacy personnel shall be trained to bring any QRE to the attention of the pharmacist on duty or the pharmacist Manager of Record immediately upon discovery.

The pharmacist who discovered or was informed of a QRE shall immediately provide notification, directions for correcting the error and instructions for minimising the negative impact on the patient; the professional-judgment qualifier applies to the prescriber notification alone.

Initial QRE documentation is due within 24 hours after the QRE is discovered by or described to the pharmacist, so the deadline is elapsed hours from discovery rather than a business-day deadline from the dispensing.

QRE documentation must describe the event sufficiently to permit categorisation and analysis and must carry the four elements listed in 247 CMR 15.03(2)(b), including the name of the person who notified the pharmacy.

QRE data shall be analysed individually and collectively to assess cause and contributing factors such as system or process failures, and the assessment must reach workflow processes, technological support, personnel training and staffing levels.
247 CMR 15.03(3)(b) requires each pharmacy to inform pharmacy personnel of changes to policies, procedures, systems or processes resulting from recommendations generated by the CQI Program.
A Manager of Record reports improper dispensing of a prescription drug resulting in serious injury or death to the Board within seven business days of discovery of that serious injury or death.

A serious adverse drug event from a drug manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy goes to the Board, the Federal Food and Drug Administration MedWatch Program and the Betsy Lehman Center for Patient Safety and Medical Error Reduction within seven business days of the knowledge of the event by any pharmacy employee.

247 CMR 20.02(3) states that the duty to report to the Board is in addition to the Continuous Quality Improvement Program requirements of 247 CMR 15.00, so the two tracks run in parallel on their own clocks.

All records relating to a reportable improper dispensing or a serious adverse drug event are kept a minimum period of five years from the date the report is filed with the Board, and shall be readily retrievable.

105 CMR 700.008 requires a registrant to report theft, loss or suspected tampering of any controlled substances to the Drug Control Program within the Department within 24 hours of discovery, on the form the Drug Control Program provides or approves.

Registrant in 105 CMR 700.000 means a person registered by the Department under M.G.L. c. 94C; a retail drug business registers with the Board instead, under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(a) and 105 CMR 700.004(A)(1).

247 CMR 20.03(7) requires a Drug Store pharmacy, sterile compounding pharmacy, complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy or nuclear pharmacy located in Massachusetts to submit to the Board a copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and DEA Form 106 within seven days of a theft or loss of a significant amount of controlled substances.
247 CMR 15.04(2) requires each pharmacy to maintain a record of all QREs for a minimum period of two years from the date of the QRE report.

247 CMR 15.04 also requires a written copy of the CQI Program description on the pharmacy premises and readily available to all pharmacy personnel, requires QRE records to be maintained in an orderly manner and filed by date, and permits QRE records to be stored at a site other than the pharmacy where the QRE occurred.

247 CMR 20.02(5) provides that the reporting requirements in 247 CMR 20.02 do not apply to non-resident pharmacies, while 247 CMR 20.07(1) requires a non-resident pharmacy to comply with all provisions of 247 CMR 20.00 unless otherwise provided.

247 CMR 20.07(3) requires a non-resident pharmacy to report to the Board any improper dispensing, into Massachusetts, of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death within seven business days of discovery of the improper dispensing.

The five-year readily retrievable retention in 247 CMR 20.02(4) requires records rather than a report, so it is not among the reporting requirements named in 247 CMR 20.02(5) and it reaches a non-resident pharmacy through 247 CMR 20.07(1), measured from the filing of that pharmacy's 247 CMR 20.07(3) report.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15 requires a person registered to dispense controlled substances who must file a DEA Form 106 with the United States Drug Enforcement Administration to file a copy simultaneously with the police department in the city or town wherein the theft or loss is alleged to have occurred and with the department of state police; a person registered to distribute files the copy with the department of state police.

105 CMR 700.004(A)(2) lists a Pharmacist among the practitioners required to be registered under 105 CMR 700.004(A)(1), separately for each business or professional activity, so an individual pharmacist holds a Department registration even though the pharmacy itself registers with the Board.

decision_logic.condition: Any member of pharmacy personnel becomes aware of a quality-related event.
decision_logic.action: Escalate immediately to the pharmacist on duty or the pharmacist Manager of Record, because 247 CMR 15.03(1) places the escalation duty on all pharmacy personnel and attaches it to discovery.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacist has discovered or been informed of a QRE.
decision_logic.action: Provide all three immediate items at once: notification to the patient or the patient's representative and to other members of the healthcare team, with the prescriber added where the pharmacist's professional judgment indicates it; directions for correcting the error; and instructions for minimising the negative impact on the patient.

decision_logic.condition: The immediate response to a QRE is under way and the pharmacist asks when the paperwork is due.
decision_logic.action: Count 24 hours from the moment the QRE was discovered by or described to that pharmacist, and build the record around the four content elements in 247 CMR 15.03(2)(b) rather than around a bare note of what happened.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacy has collected data on a set of QREs and asks what to do with it.
decision_logic.action: Analyse it individually and collectively for cause and contributing factors, cover workflow processes, technological support, personnel training and staffing levels, record any recommended remedial changes and the indicators, and then inform pharmacy personnel of the changes that result.

decision_logic.condition: An improper dispensing of a prescription drug has resulted in serious injury or death.
decision_logic.action: Identify the Manager of Record as the reporter, date the seven business days from discovery of the serious injury or death related to the improper dispensing, and do not treat the internal CQI record as a substitute for the report.

decision_logic.condition: A serious adverse drug event follows a patient's interaction with a drug manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Find the earliest point at which any pharmacy employee had knowledge of the event, count seven business days from there, and address the report to the Board, the Federal Food and Drug Administration MedWatch Program and the Betsy Lehman Center for Patient Safety and Medical Error Reduction.

decision_logic.condition: A serious-event report has been filed and the pharmacy asks how long the file must be kept.
decision_logic.action: Count a minimum of five years from the date the report was filed with the Board, keep every record relating to the event and not only the report, and store them so that they remain readily retrievable.

decision_logic.condition: Controlled substances are missing, or a container or shipment shows signs of interference.
decision_logic.action: Treat suspicion of tampering as sufficient and start 24 hours at the moment of discovery. Where the operator holds a Department registration, the report goes to the Drug Control Program within the Department on the form it provides or approves, and a Board report is not a substitute for it.

decision_logic.condition: The missing controlled substances turn out to be a theft or loss of a significant amount at a Massachusetts pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Add the Board report: submit a copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and DEA Form 106 to the Board within seven days of the theft or significant loss, and comply where applicable with the DEA, Department and state and local police requirements.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacy in the facts is a non-resident pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Apply 247 CMR 20.07(3) rather than 247 CMR 20.02(1), because 247 CMR 20.02(5) sets aside the reporting requirements in 247 CMR 20.02, and count seven business days from discovery of the improper dispensing. Then keep everything the carve-out did not name: 247 CMR 20.07(1) leaves all provisions of 247 CMR 20.00 on the pharmacy unless otherwise provided, so the five-year readily retrievable retention in 247 CMR 20.02(4) still runs, and the whole of 247 CMR 15.00 is untouched.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacy asks how long to keep the file on a quality-related event.
decision_logic.action: Keep the QRE record a minimum of two years from the date of the QRE report, filed by date and in an orderly manner, and where the event was also reportable keep all records relating to it a minimum of five years from the date the report was filed with the Board.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacy asks whether its quality assurance arrangements satisfy 247 CMR 15.00.
decision_logic.action: Walk the six minimum provisions of 247 CMR 15.02(1) one at a time, and check separately that ongoing CQI education has been provided to pharmacy personnel within the past year.

ma_vs_federal.text: 247 CMR 20.02(2) is a Massachusetts duty with a federal recipient inside it: the serious adverse drug event report goes to the Federal Food and Drug Administration MedWatch Program as well as to the Board and to the Betsy Lehman Center for Patient Safety and Medical Error Reduction. Reporting to a federal programme therefore does not indicate that the duty itself is federal.

105 CMR 700.008 is a Massachusetts Department of Public Health obligation owed to the Drug Control Program within the Department on a form that programme provides or approves. The federal theft-or-loss reporting route has its own recipient, instrument and trigger and is taught in a separate section, so satisfying one does not answer for the other.

exceptions.text: Prescriber notification is the only discretionary element in the immediate response: 247 CMR 15.03(1)(a) conditions it on the professional judgment of the pharmacist, while notification to the patient or the patient's representative and to other members of the healthcare team carries no such condition.

The same professional-judgment qualifier reappears inside the documentation content list, where 247 CMR 15.03(2)(b)4. requires documentation of the contact with the prescribing practitioner if indicated in the professional judgment of the pharmacist.

247 CMR 20.02(2) is narrower than a general adverse-event duty. It reaches a serious adverse drug event occurring as a result of a patient's interaction with any drug or pharmaceutical manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy, which is a condition on the product's origin rather than on its severity.
105 CMR 700.008 carries no confirmation exception. Suspected tampering is itself a trigger, and the regulation states no threshold, no waiting period and no exemption of its own.

That silence in the regulation is not the whole picture, because 105 CMR 700.140 lets the Commissioner waive one or more of the requirements imposed through 105 CMR 700.000, which includes 105 CMR 700.008, upon findings of undue hardship to the registrant, no jeopardy to the health or safety of individuals or the public, compensating measures acceptable to the Commissioner, and written documentation from the registrant supporting the request. It is a route to ask rather than a right to relief.

247 CMR 20.02(5) is an express carve-out, and its own words fix how far it reaches: the reporting requirements in 247 CMR 20.02 do not apply to non-resident pharmacies. It does not leave them unregulated, because 247 CMR 20.07(1) requires compliance with all provisions of 247 CMR 20.00 unless otherwise provided and 247 CMR 20.07(3) supplies a replacement duty with its own trigger. Nor does it reach a provision of 247 CMR 20.02 that requires no report: the five-year readily retrievable retention in 247 CMR 20.02(4) is a records duty, so it stays on a non-resident pharmacy.

The carve-out sits inside 247 CMR 20.02 and does not touch 247 CMR 15.00 at all, so a non-resident pharmacy's CQI Program, its 24-hour QRE documentation and its two-year QRE records are untouched by it.

The two-year QRE retention in 247 CMR 15.04(2) is expressed as a minimum period, so it is a floor rather than a destruction date, and where the same event is also a reportable serious event the five-year period in 247 CMR 20.02(4) runs alongside it on records relating to that event.

The five-year retention in 247 CMR 20.02(4) is expressed as a minimum period, so it is a floor rather than a scheduled destruction date, and it does not authorise disposal of anything a different obligation requires to be kept longer.

That is the better reading of 247 CMR 20.02(5) rather than the only possible one, since the words could be pressed as a loose reference to the whole of a section headed as a duty to report. Nothing practical turns on resolving it: a non-resident pharmacy that keeps the file five years from the filing of its 247 CMR 20.07(3) report has complied on either reading, and one that destroys it earlier has no answer if the narrower reading is right.

timing_deadlines.event: Pharmacy personnel bring a QRE to the pharmacist on duty or the pharmacist Manager of Record
timing_deadlines.consequence: The escalation duty under 247 CMR 15.03(1) sits on all pharmacy personnel, so a technician or clerk who holds an observation until a later shift has already missed it.

timing_deadlines.event: The pharmacist's response after discovering or being informed of a QRE
timing_deadlines.consequence: Notification, directions for correcting the error and instructions for minimising the negative impact on the patient are all owed at once, and none of them may be held back pending the analysis.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within 24 hours after the QRE is discovered by or described to the pharmacist
timing_deadlines.consequence: The deadline is elapsed hours from discovery or description, so it does not extend to the next business day and does not wait for confirmation of patient harm.

timing_deadlines.event: Ongoing education in the area of CQI for pharmacy personnel
timing_deadlines.consequence: A programme that trains only at induction fails 247 CMR 15.02(1)(f) however thorough the induction is.

timing_deadlines.event: The period over which the CQI Program measures its own standards
timing_deadlines.timeframe: A designated period of time chosen by the pharmacy
timing_deadlines.consequence: 247 CMR 15.03(3)(a)3. requires the analysis to develop indicators that identify means against which the programme intends to measure its standards over that period, so the period has to be designated rather than left open.

timing_deadlines.event: Report by a Manager of Record of improper dispensing of a prescription drug resulting in serious injury or death
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within seven business days of discovery of the serious injury or death related to the improper dispensing
timing_deadlines.consequence: The clock starts at discovery of the serious injury or death, not at the dispensing and not at a patient complaint, and the report goes to the Board.

timing_deadlines.event: Report by a Manager of Record of a serious adverse drug event from a drug manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within seven business days of the knowledge of the serious adverse drug event by any pharmacy employee
timing_deadlines.consequence: The period can be well advanced before the Manager of Record learns anything, and the report is owed to the Board, the Federal Food and Drug Administration MedWatch Program and the Betsy Lehman Center for Patient Safety and Medical Error Reduction.

timing_deadlines.event: Retention of records relating to a reportable improper dispensing or serious adverse drug event
timing_deadlines.timeframe: A minimum period of five years from the date the report is filed with the Board
timing_deadlines.consequence: Retention is measured from filing rather than from the event, and the records shall be readily retrievable throughout.

timing_deadlines.event: Report of theft, loss or suspected tampering of any controlled substances
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within 24 hours of discovery of the theft, loss or suspected tampering
timing_deadlines.consequence: The report is owed by a registrant of the Department to the Drug Control Program on the form it provides or approves, and suspicion of tampering starts the period without any confirmed shortfall.

timing_deadlines.event: Board report of a theft or loss of a significant amount of controlled substances at a Massachusetts pharmacy
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within seven days of such theft or significant loss
timing_deadlines.consequence: A copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and DEA Form 106 goes to the Board, so the Drug Control Program's 24-hour form is not the only Massachusetts instrument a loss can generate.

timing_deadlines.event: Retention of the record of a Quality Related Event
timing_deadlines.timeframe: A minimum period of two years from the date of the QRE report
timing_deadlines.consequence: The clock runs from the QRE report rather than from the event or from any Board filing, and the records are kept in an orderly manner and filed by date.

timing_deadlines.event: Report by a non-resident pharmacy of improper dispensing into Massachusetts resulting in serious injury or death
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within seven business days of discovery of the improper dispensing
timing_deadlines.consequence: The period starts earlier than the resident pharmacy's, which runs from discovery of the serious injury or death, because 247 CMR 20.02(5) sets aside the reporting requirements in 247 CMR 20.02 and 247 CMR 20.07(3) supplies the trigger in their place.

timing_deadlines.event: Retention by a non-resident pharmacy of records relating to an improper dispensing reported under 247 CMR 20.07(3)
timing_deadlines.timeframe: A minimum period of five years from the date the report is filed with the Board
timing_deadlines.consequence: 247 CMR 20.02(4) requires records rather than a report, so it is not among the reporting requirements named in 247 CMR 20.02(5), and 247 CMR 20.07(1) keeps it on a non-resident pharmacy together with the readily retrievable standard.

forms_records.text: QRE documentation must describe the event sufficiently to permit categorisation and analysis of it, and must include the date when the pharmacist discovered or received notification of the QRE and the name of the person who notified the pharmacy; the names and titles of the persons recording the QRE information and performing the QRE analysis; a description of the QRE reviewed; and documentation of the contact with the patient or the patient's representative, the prescribing practitioner where the pharmacist's professional judgment indicates it, and other members of the healthcare team.

The QRE analysis and assessment record must include a consideration of the effects on quality assurance related to workflow processes, technological support, personnel training and staffing levels; any recommended remedial changes to pharmacy policies, procedures, systems or processes; and the development of indicators that identify means against which the pharmacy's program intends to measure its standards over a designated period of time.

The CQI Program itself must contain a provision designating an individual or individuals responsible for monitoring CQI Program compliance with the requirements of 247 CMR 15.00, so the designation is part of the programme rather than an informal understanding about who follows up on incidents.

The serious-event file is defined by subject matter rather than by document type: all records relating to the improper dispensing of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death, and all records relating to serious adverse drug events, are retained a minimum period of five years from the date the report is filed with the Board and shall be readily retrievable. The same file is required of a non-resident pharmacy, because 247 CMR 20.02(4) requires records rather than a report and so is not among the reporting requirements named in 247 CMR 20.02(5).

The theft, loss or suspected tampering report has a prescribed instrument: it is made by completing and submitting the form provided or approved by the Drug Control Program for such purpose, so an entry in an internal log or a telephone call is not the report the regulation requires.

The Board's theft or loss report has its own instrument as well: a copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance together with a copy of the DEA Form 106, submitted to the Board within seven days of the theft or significant loss.
The CQI Program description is itself a required record: a written copy is maintained on the pharmacy premises and is readily available to all pharmacy personnel.

The QRE file has its own retention and filing standard: a minimum period of two years from the date of the QRE report, maintained in an orderly manner and filed by date, and it may be stored at a site other than the pharmacy where the QRE occurred.

The police copies have no instrument of their own. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15 requires a copy of the DEA Form 106 itself, filed simultaneously with the filing that goes to the United States Drug Enforcement Administration, so there is no separate Massachusetts police form and no separate period to count.

role_duties.duty: Be trained to bring any QRE to the attention of the pharmacist on duty or the pharmacist Manager of Record immediately upon discovery.

role_duties.role: The pharmacist who has discovered or been informed of a QRE
role_duties.duty: Immediately provide notification to the patient or the patient's representative, to the prescriber where professional judgment indicates it and to other members of the healthcare team, together with directions for correcting the error and instructions for minimising the negative impact on the patient.

role_duties.role: The pharmacist who has discovered or been informed of a QRE
role_duties.duty: Initially document the QRE within 24 hours after it is discovered by or described to that pharmacist, in a record that carries the four content elements of 247 CMR 15.03(2)(b).
Establish a Continuous Quality Improvement Program for detecting, documenting, assessing and preventing Quality Related Events, containing at a minimum the six provisions listed in 247 CMR 15.02(1).

role_duties.role: The individual or individuals designated under 247 CMR 15.02(1)(a)
role_duties.duty: Monitor CQI Program compliance with the requirements of 247 CMR 15.00.

role_duties.role: The pharmacy, through its CQI Program
role_duties.duty: Provide ongoing education at least annually in the area of CQI to pharmacy personnel.
Analyse the investigative and other pertinent data collected in response to QREs, individually and collectively, to assess the cause and any contributing factors such as system or process failures.
Inform pharmacy personnel of changes to pharmacy policies, procedures, systems or processes resulting from recommendations generated by the CQI Program.
Report to the Board any improper dispensing of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death within seven business days of discovery of that serious injury or death.

Report a serious adverse drug event arising from a drug or pharmaceutical manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy to the Board, the Federal Food and Drug Administration MedWatch Program and the Betsy Lehman Center for Patient Safety and Medical Error Reduction, within seven business days of the knowledge of the event by any pharmacy employee.

Retain all records relating to reportable improper dispensing and to serious adverse drug events for a minimum period of five years from the date the report is filed with the Board, and keep them readily retrievable.

Report the theft, loss or suspected tampering of any controlled substances to the Drug Control Program within the Department within 24 hours of discovery, on the form that programme provides or approves.

role_duties.role: A Drug Store, sterile compounding, complex non-sterile compounding or nuclear pharmacy located in Massachusetts
role_duties.duty: Report a theft or loss of a significant amount of controlled substances by submitting to the Board a copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and DEA Form 106 within seven days, and comply where applicable with the DEA, Department and state and local police requirements.

Report to the Board any improper dispensing, into Massachusetts, of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death within seven business days of discovery of the improper dispensing, and comply with all provisions of 247 CMR 20.00 unless otherwise provided, which includes retaining all records relating to that improper dispensing a minimum of five years from the date the report is filed with the Board and keeping them readily retrievable.

role_duties.role: The pharmacy, as keeper of the CQI file
role_duties.duty: Maintain a written copy of the CQI Program description on the premises and readily available to all pharmacy personnel, and maintain the record of all QREs for a minimum of two years from the date of the QRE report, in an orderly manner and filed by date.

role_duties.role: A person registered to dispense controlled substances who must file a DEA Form 106
role_duties.duty: Simultaneously file a copy of that form with the police department in the city or town wherein the theft or loss is alleged to have occurred and with the department of state police; a person registered to distribute files the copy with the department of state police.

Register with the Department under 105 CMR 700.004(A)(2), separately for each business or professional activity, so that a duty 105 CMR 700.000 places on a registrant can reach the pharmacist personally.

common_traps.text: Treating an incident log as a CQI Program. 247 CMR 15.02(1) lists six minimum provisions, and identifying and documenting QREs is only the second of them.

Reading the professional-judgment qualifier as covering the whole of the immediate response. It attaches to the prescriber notification alone; notification of the patient or the patient's representative is unconditional.

Inventing a sequence for the immediate response. 247 CMR 15.03(1) requires notification, correction directions and harm-minimisation instructions to be provided immediately, and states no order among them.
Converting the 24-hour documentation deadline into the end of the next business day, or starting it at the dispensing rather than at the discovery of or notification about the QRE.
Treating the QRE record as a free-text note. 247 CMR 15.03(2)(b) prescribes a sufficiency standard and four content elements, including the name of the person who notified the pharmacy.

Stopping the analysis at cause. 247 CMR 15.03(3)(b) requires the pharmacy to inform pharmacy personnel of the changes that result, so an analysis whose conclusions never reach the staff leaves the response half of the subsection undone.

Substituting an individual pharmacist's continuing education for the pharmacy's annual CQI education, or providing that education to pharmacists only when 247 CMR 15.02(1)(f) names pharmacy personnel.
Treating a complete CQI file as discharging the Board report. 247 CMR 20.02(3) makes the reporting duty additional to the requirements of 247 CMR 15.00, so the two tracks run in parallel.

Sending a serious adverse drug event report to the Board alone. 247 CMR 20.02(2) names three recipients, and running its clock from the Manager of Record's own knowledge instead of from any pharmacy employee's knowledge compounds the error.

Measuring the five-year retention from the dispensing, the injury or the discovery. 247 CMR 20.02(4) measures it from the date the report is filed with the Board, and it reaches all records relating to the event rather than the filed report alone.

Waiting for confirmation before reporting suspected tampering, running the 24 hours from the underlying event rather than from discovery, or sending the Drug Control Program's report to the Board of Registration in Pharmacy instead.

Turning that misdirection into a general rule that a theft or loss never goes to the Board, when 247 CMR 20.03(7) requires a copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and DEA Form 106 within seven days of a significant loss at a Massachusetts pharmacy.

Carrying the 247 CMR 20.02(1) trigger onto non-resident facts, when 247 CMR 20.02(5) sets aside the reporting requirements in 247 CMR 20.02 and 247 CMR 20.07(3) starts its seven business days at discovery of the improper dispensing.
Assuming a QRE record has no retention period, or answering with the five-year serious-event figure, when 247 CMR 15.04(2) sets a minimum of two years from the date of the QRE report.
Measuring the two-year QRE period from the event or from the Board filing, when 247 CMR 15.04(2) measures it from the date of the QRE report.

Assuming that an internal quality record is confidential or beyond discovery because it belongs to the CQI Program. The rules taught in this section confer no such protection, and none should be read into either retention period.

Reading 247 CMR 20.02(5) as lifting the whole of 247 CMR 20.02 off a non-resident pharmacy and then purging the file early. The sentence names the reporting requirements in 247 CMR 20.02; 247 CMR 20.02(4) requires records rather than a report, and 247 CMR 20.07(1) keeps it on the pharmacy, so the five-year readily retrievable period still runs.
